resources.title: My Advice for Anyone Getting Started in Photography
resources.excerpt: Ten practical tips for getting started, plus a plain-language guide to aperture, shutter speed, and ISO.
introduction: When you’re first getting started in photography, it can feel overwhelming. There are so many cameras, lenses, settings, techniques, and opinions about what you should be doing.
But becoming a better photographer doesn’t have to be complicated.
I’ve learned a lot through years of taking photos, experimenting, making mistakes, and figuring out what works for me. I’m still learning all the time.
These are ten things I’d recommend to anyone getting started in photography, along with a simple guide to understanding some of your camera’s most important settings.

sections.heading: 1. Take Lots of Photos. Seriously, Lots.
blocks: The best way to improve your photography is to take photos. A lot of them.
Don’t wait for the perfect location, perfect lighting, or perfect subject. Get outside, bring your camera, and start photographing whatever catches your attention.
The more photos you take, the more opportunities you have to experiment, make mistakes, and discover what works.

One of the most valuable things I’ve done for my photography was challenging myself to take photos every single day for a year. It pushed me to find interesting things in ordinary places and made photography part of my daily routine.
You don’t need every photo to be great. You just need to keep taking them.

sections.heading: 2. Don’t Get Caught Up in Camera Gear
blocks: You don’t need an expensive camera or a collection of lenses to become a good photographer.

It’s easy to fall into the trap of thinking a new camera or lens will make your photos better. While equipment can certainly help in specific situations, learning how to use what you already have is far more important.
Start with one camera and get comfortable with it. Ideally, use something that allows you to adjust settings manually so you can experiment with how your camera works.
But even your phone is a great place to start. You can learn an incredible amount about composition, lighting, and finding interesting subjects without buying any additional equipment.
Focus on developing your skills before investing in more gear.

sections.heading: 3. Learn the Exposure Triangle
blocks: Understanding aperture, shutter speed, and ISO is one of the most useful things you can learn when starting photography.
These three settings work together to control the brightness of your photographs, but they also influence how your images look.
Aperture affects depth of field, shutter speed controls how movement is captured, and ISO helps you work in different lighting conditions.
You don’t need to master all three immediately. Start by understanding what each setting does and experiment with changing them.
Try photographing the same subject with different settings and compare the results.
I’ve included a simple explanation of these settings later in this guide.

sections.heading: 4. Pay Attention to Composition
blocks: Composition is about deciding what goes into your photograph and how everything is arranged within the frame.
Before taking a photo, think about what you’re trying to capture. What’s the subject? Is there anything distracting in the background? Would the photo look better from a different angle?
Sometimes moving a few steps to the left or right can completely change a photograph.
Experiment with getting closer to your subject, photographing from lower angles, or including more of the environment.
You can also explore techniques like leading lines, framing, symmetry, and the rule of thirds.
But don’t feel like you need to follow composition rules all the time. They’re useful tools, not requirements.

sections.heading: 5. Learn to See Light
blocks: Light is one of the most important elements of photography.
Start paying attention to how light changes throughout the day and how it affects the things around you.
Morning and evening sunlight can create beautiful colors and long shadows. Midday sunlight can produce strong contrast and harsh shadows. Overcast days provide softer, more even lighting.
None of these conditions is necessarily better than another. They simply create different opportunities.
Look at where the light is coming from, how it falls on your subject, and what happens in the shadows.
I personally love working with strong sunlight, bold shadows, and vibrant colors. Learning to recognize those conditions has become an important part of how I approach photography.
The more you pay attention to light, the more you’ll start noticing photographic opportunities everywhere.

sections.heading: 6. Look Back at Your Photographs
blocks: Taking photos is important, but reviewing them is just as valuable.
Spend time looking through the photographs you’ve taken. Don’t just focus on the ones you like.
Ask yourself why certain photos work and why others don’t.
Was the composition interesting? Was the subject in focus? Did the lighting help or hurt the image? Was there something distracting in the background?
Think about what you would do differently if you could take the photograph again.
You might discover that you consistently prefer certain compositions, lighting conditions, or subjects.
Looking back at older work can also be incredibly rewarding because it allows you to see how much you’ve improved.

sections.heading: 7. Photograph What Interests You
blocks: Don’t worry about finding your photography style right away.
When you’re starting out, experiment with photographing all kinds of subjects.
Try street photography, landscapes, architecture, portraits, cars, nature, or anything else that catches your attention.
Pay attention to what you enjoy photographing and what makes you excited to pick up your camera.
Over time, you’ll start noticing patterns in your work.

For me, color has become a huge part of my photography. I love finding interesting combinations of colors, architecture, and light. But that developed through years of experimenting with different subjects and approaches.
Your style doesn’t need to be something you consciously decide on. It can develop naturally through the photographs you enjoy making.

sections.heading: 8. Experiment With Editing
blocks: Editing is another important part of the creative process.
Taking a photograph is only one part of creating the final image. Editing allows you to refine how the photograph looks and feels.
Start by experimenting with simple adjustments like exposure, contrast, highlights, shadows, white balance, and color.
Pay attention to how each adjustment changes your photograph.
You don’t need expensive editing software to get started. There are plenty of tools available, including free options.
Presets can be useful, but I’d encourage you to learn what the individual adjustments actually do rather than relying entirely on someone else’s editing style.
Over time, editing can become another way to develop your own creative approach to photography.

sections.heading: 9. Study Other Photographers
blocks: One of the best ways to learn photography is to look at the work of other photographers.
Find photographers whose work you admire and spend time studying their images.
Instead of simply thinking a photograph looks great, ask yourself why.
Is it the composition? The lighting? The colors? The subject? The moment they captured?
Look at how different photographers approach similar subjects and what makes their work unique.
Photography books, exhibitions, websites, and social media can all be great sources of inspiration.
Don’t feel like you need to copy someone else’s style. Use their work to discover new techniques, ideas, and ways of seeing the world.

sections.heading: 10. Enjoy the Process
blocks: Photography should be something you enjoy.
It’s easy to get caught up in comparing your photographs to other people’s work, worrying about social media engagement, or feeling like every photo needs to be amazing.
Try not to let those things take away from the experience.
Go somewhere new. Explore your neighborhood. Take photos of ordinary things. Experiment with techniques you’ve never tried before.
Some days you’ll come home with photographs you love. Other days you might not get anything worth keeping.
That’s all part of the process.
You don’t need to share every photograph you take, and you don’t need every photography outing to produce something incredible.
Just keep exploring, experimenting, and enjoying the experience of making photographs.

sections.heading: Understanding Your Camera’s Settings
blocks: If you’re new to photography, camera settings can seem intimidating. You’ll see terms like aperture, shutter speed, ISO, and exposure, along with a bunch of numbers that might not mean much at first.
The good news is that you don’t need to understand every camera setting to start taking great photographs.
Three of the most important settings to learn are aperture, shutter speed, and ISO. Together, they’re commonly called the exposure triangle.
Each setting affects the brightness of your photograph, but they also have different creative effects.
Here’s a simple breakdown.

link.description: Keep this field reference handy when bright, dark, or vivid subjects throw off your camera’s meter.

subsections.heading: Aperture
blocks: Aperture controls the size of the opening inside your lens that allows light to reach your camera’s sensor.
A lower f-number, like f/1.8, means a wider opening that lets in more light. A higher f-number, like f/16, means a smaller opening that lets in less light.
Aperture also affects something called depth of field, which describes how much of your scene appears acceptably sharp.

points: Low f-number (f/1.8): More light, shallower depth of field, and potentially blurrier backgrounds.
Medium f-number (f/4): A balance between depth of field and light.
High f-number (f/8–f/16): Less light and generally more of the scene appearing in focus.

blocks: If you’re photographing a person and want a blurry background, you might choose a wider aperture like f/1.8.
If you’re photographing a landscape and want more of the scene in focus, you might choose something like f/8.
The available apertures depend on your lens.

subsections.heading: Shutter Speed
blocks: Shutter speed controls how long your camera’s sensor is exposed to light.
A fast shutter speed captures a very short moment in time, while a slow shutter speed allows light to reach the sensor for longer.
Shutter speed also determines how movement appears in your photographs.

points: Fast (1/1000): Great for freezing fast-moving subjects like sports, cars, or animals.
Medium (1/250): Useful for everyday photography and capturing people moving.
Slow (1/30): Can introduce motion blur or camera shake, especially when shooting handheld.
Very slow (1 second or longer): Useful for long exposures, light trails, or creative motion effects, usually with a tripod.

blocks: For example, if you’re photographing someone riding a bicycle, a fast shutter speed can freeze them in motion.
But if you want to capture a sense of movement, a slower shutter speed can create intentional motion blur.

subsections.heading: ISO
blocks: ISO controls how your camera responds to the light captured by the sensor.
Increasing ISO makes your photograph brighter when aperture and shutter speed stay the same, which can be helpful when photographing in darker environments.
However, higher ISO settings can also introduce more noise, which may appear as grain or unwanted color variations in your photographs.

points: ISO 100: Great for bright conditions and generally produces very clean images.
ISO 400–800: Useful for cloudy days, shade, or moderately low-light environments.
ISO 1600–3200+: Helpful in darker conditions when you need to maintain a faster shutter speed.

blocks: Modern cameras can often handle higher ISO settings surprisingly well, so don’t be afraid to increase ISO when you need to.
A sharp photograph with a little noise is often better than a blurry photograph caused by using a shutter speed that’s too slow.

subsections.heading: How the Three Settings Work Together
blocks: Aperture, shutter speed, and ISO all influence exposure, which is how bright or dark your photograph appears.
Changing one setting often means adjusting another to maintain the brightness you want.
For example, using a faster shutter speed means less light reaches the sensor. You might compensate by using a wider aperture or increasing ISO.
The important thing to understand is that these settings aren’t just about making your photographs brighter or darker.
They’re creative tools that allow you to control depth of field, movement, and how your camera handles different lighting conditions.
You don’t need to shoot in full manual mode all the time to learn them, either.
Try using Aperture Priority (Av or A) to experiment with depth of field, or Shutter Priority (Tv or S) to explore how movement appears in your photographs.
These modes allow you to control one setting while your camera helps manage the exposure.
The more you experiment, the more intuitive these decisions will become.

sections.heading: Final Thoughts
blocks: If there’s one thing I’d encourage anyone getting started in photography to do, it’s to keep taking photos.
You don’t need the most expensive camera, you don’t need to understand every technical detail, and you certainly don’t need every photograph to be great.
Start with what you have. Take lots of photos. Experiment with your settings, pay attention to light and composition, and spend time looking back at your work.
Most importantly, photograph things that interest you and enjoy the process.
The more you practice, the more you’ll learn, and the more your own approach to photography will develop.
Now grab your camera and go take some photos.

resources.title: What’s in My Camera Bag
resources.excerpt: A look at the camera, lenses, and lighting I’m using right now.
introduction: Here’s a look at the gear I reach for most often: my current camera, three go-to lenses, and the tripod and light I use when the shoot calls for them.
This is a snapshot of what I use right now. If you’re just getting started, the camera you already have is plenty to start making photos.

sections.heading: Camera: Canon EOS R5
blocks: The Canon EOS R5 is my current camera. I use a mix of RF and EF lenses, so moving to an RF body didn’t mean replacing every lens.

sections.heading: My go-to lenses
blocks: I keep three focal lengths in rotation: a wide 24mm, a 50mm prime, and a 100–400mm zoom for more reach.

subsections.heading: Canon RF 24mm f/1.8 Macro IS STM
blocks: The 24mm is my wide-angle option. It gives me room to show more of the street or the architecture around a subject, and it can also focus close for details.

subsections.heading: Canon EF 100–400mm f/4.5–5.6L
blocks: This is the EF version of Canon’s 100–400mm zoom. The extra reach makes it useful for picking out distant details or isolating a subject from a busy scene.

subsections.heading: Canon EF 50mm f/1.4 USM
blocks: This is still my go-to 50mm. It’s a useful middle ground when I want a tighter frame than the 24mm, and the f/1.4 aperture gives me room to work in lower light. I may swap to a newer 50mm later, but this is what I’m using today.

sections.heading: Tripod: SLIK carbon fiber
blocks: I’ve had my SLIK carbon fiber tripod for a few years. It’s the one I reach for when I need the camera to stay still, especially for slower shutter speeds.

sections.heading: Lighting: Profoto B20
blocks: The B20 is the light I reach for when I want to add flash. It’s battery powered, which is handy when I want to set up away from an outlet.
